name: PT Exploitasi Energi Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Exploitasi Energi Indonesia: a PLN coal-distribution spread priced for extinction
frontmatter.summary: Exploitasi Energi Indonesia moves coal for PLN's power plants, earning a rupiah spread on about two million tonnes a year. The spread compressed in the first half as seaborne coal rose. The shares trade near one times EBITDA because the parent has negative equity, a going-concern opinion and almost no daily volume. Our DCF, discounted for illiquidity, supports a BUY.
thesis: CNKO is a distribution business, not a miner: it buys coal, mostly from one supplier, and delivers it to two PLN generation subsidiaries, so the earnings driver is tonnes times spread rather than a reserve [S3, S4].
The spread is cyclical and only partly contractual: FY2025 gross margin of 20.4% falls to 11.5% in our FY2026 estimate because the purchase cost rose faster than the PLN tariff [S3, S4].

The balance sheet, not the earnings, sets the price: parent equity was IDR-1,037.6bn at the end of FY2025, the auditor flagged material going-concern uncertainty, and a dividend declared more than a decade ago remains unpaid [S3].
Cash is real but encumbered: IDR336.6bn of the IDR338.3bn cash sits at the bank that lends to the group, the bank loan is secured on the PLN receivables, and the factoring line is with recourse [S4].

At Rp37 the market capitalisation is IDR331.4bn against IDR334.8bn of FY2025 EBITDA; our DCF gives Rp246 and the weighted target Rp193, a 420.4% return. The bear case is nil, because it assumes the PLN contract is not renewed and the capital deficiency is closed at a distressed price [S0, S3].

blocks.text: **Rating: BUY · target Rp193 · last close Rp37 · return 420.4%**

This round answers the red team: the market-cap unit and the FY2025 equity period are corrected, the DCF now stops at the October 2029 contract expiry, the payables and receivables are quantified, and the bear case is rebuilt to a nil equity value.

PT Exploitasi Energi Indonesia Tbk buys thermal coal and delivers it to two subsidiaries of the state electricity utility. In FY2025 it sold 2,153.3 thousand tonnes, of which 59.1% went to PT PLN Indonesia Power and 40.0% to PT PLN Nusantara Power; the two together are effectively the entire revenue line [S3]. The coal comes overwhelmingly from third parties, with purchases from PT Borneo Indobara alone equal to 55.9% of revenue [S3]. CNKO owns no producing mine: neither of the two concessions it has held was ever operated, and one of them was sold in April 2026 [S3, S8]. This is a volume-and-spread distribution business with a contract book, a leased logistics chain and a very thin equity cushion.

The FY2025 economics look excellent at first sight. Revenue was IDR1,863.6bn, gross profit IDR380.3bn, EBITDA IDR334.8bn and net profit attributable to shareholders IDR194.6bn, with free cash flow of IDR217.7bn [S3]. Capital expenditure was only IDR0.7bn because the fleet is leased and the plant is small [S3]. On a market capitalisation of IDR331.4bn the enterprise value is 1.4x FY2025 EBITDA and the shares trade at 1.7x earnings [S0].

The reason is the balance sheet. The group ended FY2025 with a capital deficiency of IDR1,064.3bn, current liabilities exceeding current assets by IDR783.1bn, and parent equity of IDR-1,037.6bn [S3]. The auditor, Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, a BDO member firm, signed an unmodified opinion but added a material-uncertainty paragraph on going concern [S3]. At June 2026 the parent equity was still negative at IDR-940.8bn [S4]. Cash of IDR338.3bn is real, but IDR336.6bn of it is deposited at PT Bank Sinarmas, which is also the group's bank lender, and the loan is secured on the PLN receivables [S4]. The shares trade at a three-month average daily value of IDR0.0bn, and the exchange's September 2026 list of issuers released from special monitoring does not include CNKO; absence from that list is not proof of the board status [S9].

Our view is that the operating business is worth substantially more than the price even after a full illiquidity discount, and that the market is assigning a high probability to the loss of the PLN book rather than its continuation. The first half of 2026 showed the mechanism: revenue of IDR1,023.5bn was only slightly below the IDR1,046.9bn reported a year earlier, but gross profit fell to IDR143.2bn against IDR225.9bn as the coal purchase cost rose and the domestic selling price lagged [S4]. That is a spread business passing through a commodity cycle, not a broken business. The house coal deck has Newcastle easing from US$150.3 spot to US$118.0 next year and US$110.0 the year after, which restores the gross margin toward the FY2025 level [S6].

We value CNKO on a discounted cash-flow basis only, at Rp246 per share. We tested an EV/EBITDA cross-check and rejected it: the engine strikes it on FY2025A peak EBITDA and the peer set spans a very wide range, from about three times to more than forty times, so the median is not a comparable valuation for a low-margin distributor. P/BV is meaningless with negative book. After a 30.0% illiquidity discount on the scenario-weighted value, the twelve-month target is Rp193, 420.4% above the last close [S0]. The bear case is valued at nil, because it assumes the contract is not renewed and the capital deficiency is closed at a distressed price; the bull case at Rp628 requires the spread to normalise, the contract to be renewed and part of the governance discount to close [S0].

What moves the value, in order, is the gross spread per tonne; the tonnes delivered under the PLN PJBB; and whether the market ever pays for the cash and earnings that the accounts show. The first is cyclical and already turning in our deck. The second depends on the CIF PJBB that runs to 29 October 2029, after a renewal record that goes back to 2011 [S4]. The third is the real variant: a profitable distributor with negative equity cannot return cash until it rebuilds capital, so the value has to be realised either through retained earnings or through a corporate action. We think the earnings are real enough to rebuild the equity over the forecast period; the market is not paying for that path, and the bear case shows what happens if the path fails.

Coal distribution in Indonesia is a working-capital business dressed as a commodity business. A distributor contracts volumes and qualities with a power plant, sources the coal from a concession holder, arranges barging and hauling, and is paid on delivery. It holds little inventory and is financed by a mixture of supplier credit, customer prepayment and bank or factoring lines. The accounting consequence is that a profitable distributor can show negative operating working capital, because payables to suppliers and deposits received run ahead of the cash it collects from buyers. The economic consequence is that a small change in the spread per tonne moves net profit far more than the same change would move a miner's.

PT Exploitasi Energi Indonesia Tbk is an Indonesian energy company whose revenue is dominated by coal trading and delivery, with a small captive power plant and ancillary vessel leasing [S3]. In FY2025 coal sales generated IDR1,846.0bn of revenue and the Pangkalan Bun coal-fired plant contributed IDR17.7bn [S3]. The company describes its activities as coal trading, vessel leasing and steam power generation, and the segment note confirms that coal sales are the overwhelming majority of the top line [S3]. The economic substance is simpler than the description: CNKO is a distributor that stands between a coal supplier and two power-generation buyers.

The customer book is the business. PT PLN Indonesia Power took 59.1% of FY2025 revenue and PT PLN Nusantara Power took 40.0% [S3]. The corporate website lists the plants served, all of them PLN coal stations in Java: Suralaya Baru, Labuan, Teluk Naga, Rembang, Indramayu, Adipala and Tanjung Awar-Awar [S8]. That list is a useful description of the route: coal is moved into plants on the Java grid. There is no meaningful non-PLN customer base, so the credit quality of the receivable is the credit quality of the state utility, and the volume is the volume that the utility chooses to take.

The supply side is more concentrated than the customer side. Purchases from PT Borneo Indobara were equal to 55.9% of revenue in FY2025, down from a higher share the year before [S3]. Coal purchases of IDR1,062.8bn were the largest single cost, and freight of IDR388.1bn was the next largest, together making up the bulk of cost of revenue of IDR1,483.3bn [S3]. A distributor with one dominant supplier and two dominant buyers has very little bargaining power on either side of the trade. Its negotiating position is the contract it has already signed, not a structural advantage.

Volumes are contracted, not guided down. Coal sales were 2,197.0 thousand tonnes in FY2024 and 2,153.3 thousand tonnes in FY2025, a small decline, while total shipments were 2,174.0 thousand tonnes [S2]. Management set a delivery target of 2,000 thousand tonnes for FY2026, which is the annual contract quantity under the PLN CIF PJBB [S2, S4]; the contract band admits volumes within a fifth of that quantity either way. The 2025 shipments were 14.4% above the company's own internal budget of 1,900 thousand tonnes [S2]. We therefore take the midpoint between the target and the FY2025 actual as the base case, with the bull at a repeat of the FY2025 volume and the bear at the contract floor.

The group structure contains two mining concessions, but neither is an operating asset. PT Abe Jaya Perkasa holds a concession in Central Kalimantan with 95.4 million tonnes of resources, including a hypothetical category, and PT Sekti Rahayu Indah held 73.5 million tonnes before it was sold [S8]. The annual report states that the reserves belong to the subsidiaries and that mining operations have not commenced [S3]. On 29 April 2026 the group disposed of its entire holding in PT Sekti Rahayu Indah to PT Mitra Barito and PT Banua Antang Raya for IDR50.0bn of cash, recognising a gain of IDR62.0bn [S4]. The remaining concession is dormant, but we do not value it at zero: the bridge carries it at half the value per tonne implied by the SRI transaction, probability-weighted, because there is still no mine plan, permit or funding commitment [S4, S8].

Control sits with Anderson Bay Pte Ltd, which held 45.6% at the end of FY2025 [S2]. The free float is 54.4% and insiders hold 46.1%, so the register is concentrated but not closed [S0]. The company employed 31 people at the last count, which is consistent with a trading and logistics operation that leases most of what it uses [S0]. Strategy as management describes it is to optimise deliveries under the PLN PJBB that runs to 29 October 2029, collect the sale proceeds, and keep the cost base variable; the going-concern note lists exactly that plan [S3, S4]. There is no disclosed expansion programme and no material capital commitment [S3].

The business is best understood as a tolling-like spread. CNKO does not control the coal price, the freight rate, the plant's burn or the tariff formula. It controls the contract, the logistics arrangement and, critically, the working-capital cycle. When the spread is wide, as in FY2025, the equity generates cash quickly. When the purchase cost rises faster than the tariff, as in the first half of 2026, the same tonnes produce much less gross profit [S3, S4]. That is the cycle an investor is buying, not a resource.

The sector is classified as coal distribution, part of the broader energy complex on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. The demand driver is the coal consumed by the PLN generation fleet and the independent power producers attached to it, not seaborne export demand [S2]. CNKO's customers are utility subsidiaries, and its volumes are set by their dispatch and their procurement schedules. That makes the industry look like a regulated logistics business at the point of sale and a commodity trading business at the point of purchase.

The single most important policy fact is the domestic market obligation. Coal producers must sell at least 25.0% of output to domestic buyers, and the price for coal sold to PLN and independent power producers is capped at US$70 per tonne [S6]. The government is tightening the rules, with a planned ban on using off-grid power plants to satisfy the domestic obligation in order to redirect supply to the grid [S6]. The cap is set for 6,322 kcal/kg GAR coal; CNKO's concession resources are lower grade at 5,575 kcal/kg air-dried and 4,290 kcal/kg as-received [S8], and the realised revenue per tonne is far below the cap, so the cap itself is not the binding constraint on CNKO's selling price. The binding price is the PJBB tariff, which resets with a lag and only partly passes through a seaborne move, as the first half of 2026 demonstrated [S4, S6]. The tightening that redirects off-grid supply to the grid is not only a constraint: the plants CNKO serves are grid plants, so the policy should support its PLN volumes, which we carry as an upside in the bull case rather than as an extra headwind [S6].

Seaborne prices are well above the domestic market. Newcastle spot was US$150.3 per tonne at the end of October 2026 [S6], while the government's high-GAR HBA marker was US$126.8 for the second half of October under the standing decree [S10]. The house coal deck, whose annual markers come from the World Bank Pink Sheet and Newcastle contract prints, carries Newcastle at US$118.0 for next year and US$110.0 the year after, a path that assumes the current tightness fades as Indonesian and Chinese supply responds. The reviewed HBA path tracks it closely at US$112.0 for FY2027E and US$108.0 for FY2028E, so the template's Newcastle link is not a meaningfully different price view from the Indonesian reference. The house macro deck holds thermal coal NEUTRAL and the balance of payments CAUTIOUS, so the rupiah is a headwind rather than a tailwind for a dollar-cost, rupiah-revenue distributor. The spread between the seaborne market and the domestic price is the reason CNKO's purchase cost rises faster than its selling price when the export market is strong, and the reason the margin recovers when it weakens.

The competitive landscape is fragmented at the distribution layer and concentrated at the supply layer. Dozens of Indonesian traders and logistics groups can move coal to a PLN plant, but few have the combination of a multi-year contract, a reliable supplier relationship and the balance sheet to fund the receivable. CNKO's edge is the contract book and its relationship with the two PLN subsidiaries, not a cost advantage or a proprietary asset [S2, S3]. Its weakness is that the same contract book is re-tendered, and the supplier relationship is concentrated in one counterparty accounting for more than half of revenue [S3].

The five forces are unfavourable on every axis except buyer credit quality. Supplier power is high because one supplier provides the majority of the coal [S3]. Buyer power is high because two state-owned subsidiaries account for essentially all revenue [S3]. The threat of new entrants is moderate because the capital required is working capital rather than mining equipment, but the contract relationship is the barrier. Substitutes are limited in the near term because coal-fired generation is the backbone of the Java grid, but the long-run energy transition is a structural headwind. Rivalry is intense because the product is undifferentiated and the contract is awarded on price and reliability.

Regulation and macro policy matter more than competitive strategy. The domestic price cap, the export-proceeds rules and the DMO percentage all change the relative economics of selling domestically versus exporting, and therefore the price at which CNKO can source third-party coal [S6]. The rupiah exchange rate matters because the seaborne benchmark is denominated in dollars while the selling price is in rupiah; a weaker rupiah raises the local-currency cost of imported-equivalent coal without an automatic increase in the domestic tariff [S6]. Our macro deck assumes the rupiah remains under balance-of-payments pressure, which is a headwind for the spread rather than a tailwind.

Our assessment is that CNKO has no durable moat. It has a contract, a supplier relationship and a working-capital machine. Those are worth something while they last, and they can be worth a great deal when the spread is wide, but they are not a franchise. The correct valuation frame is therefore a cash-flow model of the existing book with a conservative terminal assumption, not a multiple of peak earnings and not a resource NAV [S3].

The domestic coal market obligation exists because Indonesia exports most of its thermal coal while its power sector needs secure, cheap supply. Producers receive a lower price for the domestic share than they would in the export market, and the state utility receives a price that is insulated from seaborne rallies. Distributors sit between the two and earn a margin that widens when the domestic price lags the export price and narrows when it catches up. The policy is periodically revised, which is why contract terms and counterparty behaviour matter more than the spot price alone.

The history is a recovery story followed by a very good year. Revenue rose from IDR1,375.3bn in FY2022 to IDR1,863.6bn in FY2025, while EBIT went from IDR-80.0bn to IDR317.8bn [S0, S3]. The improvement was not driven by a structural change in the business; it was driven by a wider spread, lower freight costs and a cost base that had already been cut. FY2024 gross profit was IDR244.9bn on revenue of IDR1,731.5bn, and FY2025 gross profit rose to IDR380.3bn on revenue of IDR1,863.6bn [S3]. Operating leverage in a distribution business is brutal in both directions, which the later first-half numbers confirm.

FY2025 was the peak year in the data. Revenue of IDR1,863.6bn produced gross profit of IDR380.3bn, SG&A of IDR62.5bn, EBIT of IDR317.8bn and EBITDA of IDR334.8bn [S3]. Interest and finance charges were IDR57.7bn, tax was IDR52.3bn and net profit attributable to shareholders was IDR194.6bn [S3]. Depreciation was IDR17.0bn, most of it right-of-use amortisation on leased barges and office space rather than owned plant [S3]. The company converted a large part of that EBITDA into operating cash flow, and capital expenditure of IDR0.7bn left almost all of it available for debt service and working capital [S3].

The cost structure explains the sensitivity. Coal purchases of IDR1,062.8bn were 71.6% of cost of revenue, and freight of IDR388.1bn was the next largest line [S3]. We model the coal purchase cost as a pass-through with a lag: the company can recover 41.0% of a change in the seaborne benchmark in the selling price, and absorbs the rest in margin [S3, S4]. That calibration comes from the first half of 2026, when the Newcastle average rose while the domestic tariff did not, and gross margin fell from the FY2025 level to the low teens rather than holding flat [S4]. The first-half margin move already contains the freight and fuel squeeze, so we set the separate Brent link to 0.0%; adding it on top would double-count roughly a percentage point of the margin decline [S3, S4].

The first half of 2026 is the most important recent data point. Revenue was IDR1,023.5bn against IDR1,046.9bn in the first half of 2025, a small decline, but gross profit fell to IDR143.2bn from IDR225.9bn [S4]. Operating income was IDR106.3bn and total depreciation IDR4.1bn, so first-half EBITDA was only a little above operating income; operating cash flow was IDR102.2bn, which is why the group met its interest bill without new money [S4]. Net profit was IDR122.9bn, flattered by the IDR62.0bn gain on the sale of PT Sekti Rahayu Indah; excluding that gain, the underlying result was roughly half the prior-year run rate [S4]. The proceeds of IDR50.0bn are in the June cash balance [S4]. The message is not that the business is loss-making; it is that the spread, not the volume, drives the result, and the spread was squeezed.

Our forecast is H1 actual plus an implied second half, not a fresh run from FY2025. First-half revenue of IDR1,023.5bn and gross profit of IDR143.2bn are in the model; the second half is priced at the deck's second-half Newcastle and gives FY2026 revenue of IDR1,854.3bn and a gross margin of 11.5% [S4]. That blended margin is consistent with the first-half actual and the 41.0% pass-through: the implied second-half margin is below the first half's because the deck's second-half coal price is higher, and a nine-month margin at the first-half level would therefore be a beat, not the base case. As the deck's coal price falls to US$118.0 in FY2027, the gross margin recovers to 17.4%, EBITDA rises to IDR283.5bn and net profit to IDR178.5bn.

Working capital is the unusual feature. Operating working capital was IDR-918.4bn at the end of FY2025, or -49.3% of revenue, because trade payables and refundable security deposits run well ahead of receivables and inventory [S3]. At June 2026 current assets of IDR802.7bn against current liabilities of IDR1,525.4bn, of which trade payables were IDR956.8bn and refundable deposits IDR379.9bn, keep the ratio near the same level [S4]. That negative working capital is a source of cash when revenue grows and a use of cash when it shrinks; our model carries only the annual change, and caps the ratio as a share of revenue rather than letting the float grow faster than the business [S4]. The level is not capitalised in the enterprise value: the deposit component is separately deducted as debt-like in the bridge, and the float is unlikely to change while the PJBB is in place.

The balance sheet is the constraint. At the end of FY2025 total assets were IDR891.4bn, total liabilities IDR1,955.6bn and parent equity IDR-1,037.6bn [S3]. The group's capital deficiency was IDR1,064.3bn, and current liabilities exceeded current assets by IDR783.1bn [S3]. At June 2026 the parent equity was still IDR-940.8bn, despite the disposal gain, because the gain was accounting profit rather than a rebuild of capital [S4]. Interest-bearing debt was IDR381.8bn at the end of FY2025 and IDR350.5bn at June 2026, of which IDR258.6bn was Sinar Mas Multifinance recourse factoring and the rest a Bank Sinarmas term loan and consumer finance [S3, S4]. Cash was IDR338.3bn at June 2026, so net debt was small in absolute terms, but the cash is not freely available: most of it sits at the lending bank and the receivables are pledged [S4].

The going-concern language is unambiguous. The auditor's material-uncertainty paragraph refers to the capital deficiency and the working-capital deficit and states that these conditions may cast significant doubt on the group's ability to continue [S3]. Management's response is to optimise deliveries under the five-year PLN contract and to manage costs [S3]. We treat that as the base case because the first half of 2026 produced positive EBITDA and the group met its interest bill; a liquidity event is a tail risk, not the central path [S4]. But the tail is fat, and it is the reason the equity trades where it does.

Capital allocation is conservative by necessity. The stated dividend policy is a 40.0% payout when annual net profit exceeds a threshold, but the board paid nothing for FY2025 because of the capital position, and the unpaid dividend from FY2012 of IDR16.3bn is still on the balance sheet [S2, S3]. We assume no dividend in the forecast period, which is the most likely path given the negative equity and the bank covenants [S3]. Any cash generated goes first to debt reduction and working capital, and only then to shareholders.

Earnings quality deserves a separate word. The FY2026 result contains a one-off disposal gain, and the first-half underlying profit is materially below the reported number [S4]. Related-party balances include a receivable of IDR49.4bn that is fully impaired and a payable of IDR35.5bn to a related individual [S3]. Gross trade receivables were IDR922.1bn at June 2026 against a IDR594.5bn impairment allowance, leaving IDR327.6bn net, up from IDR114.6bn at December [S4]. The jump is a PLN billing-timing effect, not a factoring change: the with-recourse facility of IDR258.6bn is broadly unchanged, and IDR810.6bn of cash was collected from customers in the half [S4]. The receivables growth is far more than the revenue change, which is exactly the earnings-quality divergence flag; we discuss it in the risks and do not extrapolate it in the forecast, where working capital is held as a share of revenue [S4]. None of these is evidence of manipulation, but together they mean the reported profit is not a clean measure of distributable cash. We anchor the valuation on EBITDA and cash flow, not on the reported net profit.

We use a discounted cash-flow model as the sole weighted method. The industry template prescribes DCF as primary with EV/EBITDA and P/BV as checks, but a negative book value makes P/BV meaningless: parent equity was IDR-940.8bn at June 2026, so a multiple of book would produce a negative value for a business that is generating cash [S4]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on FY2025A peak EBITDA of IDR334.8bn and the peer set spans a very wide range, from about three times to more than forty times, so the median capitalises a peak year on non-comparable businesses [S0]. We therefore give the DCF the full weight and set both cross-checks to zero.

The cost of capital is high because the company is small, illiquid and levered. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5% [S0]. We use the industry default unlevered beta of 1.00, lever it at the market debt-to-equity ratio of 1.06, and add a company premium of 3.4%. That premium does two jobs: about two and a half points align the engine's macro-deck debt cost with CNKO's actual blended borrowing cost, because the Bank Sinarmas term loan is 10.5% after the February 2026 cut and the Sinar Mas with-recourse factoring is 14.0% against our 12.4% input [S4], and one point is a company-specific charge for negative equity and the going-concern paragraph [S3]. The result is a cost of equity of 21.5%, a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and a WACC of 14.2%. That WACC is deliberately conservative: a coal distributor with a state-owned customer and a variable cost base does not deserve a mid-cycle cost of capital while its equity is negative.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR2,563.8bn and an equity value per share of Rp246. The explicit forecast stops at FY2029E because the PLN CIF PJBB expires on 29 October 2029; the terminal value is 71.1% of enterprise value and capitalises a renewal that we do not take for granted [S4]. The renewal case rests on the record rather than on hope: PLN PJBBs have run since January 2011, were restated in June 2019, re-signed as the CIF contract in April 2022 and amended in August 2024 and January 2026, and the consortium agreement extends if the PJBB continues [S4]. We assign that renewal the base case; the bear case removes it and takes the equity to nil. The free cash flow is close to EBITDA because capex is negligible and working capital is a source of cash; that is the correct treatment for a distributor that leases its fleet, but it also means the model is sensitive to any change in the leasing or working-capital terms [S3]. If suppliers shorten credit or demand their deposits back, the negative working capital reverses and the value falls toward the bear case; that is the single assumption we would stress first [S4]. We discount from the June 2026 balance-sheet date and use the latest debt and cash [S4]. The four explicit contract years alone, before any terminal value, already exceed the present market capitalisation of IDR331.4bn, so the price is not relying solely on a generous post-2029 assumption.

The bridge carries two items that the operating DCF does not. First, the dormant AJP concession is not zero: the April 2026 SRI sale valued 73.5 million tonnes at IDR50.0bn, and we apply that price per tonne to AJP's 95.4 million tonnes but carry only half of it, because there is no mine plan, permit or funding commitment [S4, S8]. Second, the IDR379.9bn of refundable security deposits is treated as a debt-like claim, not as permanent equity, so a buyer who had to honour it would see that value leave the bridge [S4]. The deposits remain inside the operating working-capital ratio, but only their annual change affects cash flow, so this is not a double count of the principal.

The sensitivity is wide because the spread and the discount rate both matter. Moving the WACC by a percentage point in either direction changes the DCF value by roughly a tenth, and moving terminal growth by the same amount changes it by a similar order [S0]. A two-percentage-point change in the gross margin changes the twelve-month value by more than the current share price [S0]. The table makes the point that this is not a precise valuation; it is a range whose centre is above the market price, but whose bear tail reaches zero.

The bridge from the DCF to the target is unusual because the market value of equity is small relative to the operating value. The scenario-weighted value before the illiquidity discount is Rp275; we apply a 30.0% discount because the stock has a three-month average daily traded value of IDR0.0bn, a free float of 54.4% and a history of long suspension-like stretches [S0]. The result is Rp193. The discount is the maximum in the house framework, and even then the weighted value sits above the price. That gap is not a prediction that the shares will re-rate to the DCF; it is a statement that the market is pricing a lower renewal probability or a higher distress probability than our base case, and the bear scenario shows what that outcome is worth.

The reverse DCF makes the market's implicit view explicit. At the current price and our cost of capital, the market is discounting FY2027 revenue growth of -12.3% a year, a permanent contraction far beyond the company's own delivery target [S0, S2]. That is consistent with the market assigning a high probability to contract loss, a failed refinancing or a heavily dilutive capital raise. It is not, by itself, evidence that the market is wrong. Our variant view is that the renewal record and the first-half cash generation make that probability lower than the price implies; the bear case is the honest statement of what happens if we are wrong.

What would change the valuation is not a small move in the coal price. It is a change in the contract, a change in the capital structure, or a change in the market's willingness to hold an illiquid negative-equity name. A new multi-year PLN contract at a wider spread would lift the DCF; a rights issue or a debt-for-equity swap would dilute the per-share value, and a large raise at the current price would be close to a recapitalisation; a delisting or a suspension would make the discount irrelevant because there would be no exit. The capital structure is the swing factor: the group needs to rebuild a deficiency of IDR1,064.3bn before the equity can be valued on a normal multiple, which is why the position is sized as a deep-value special situation rather than a core holding.

The largest risk is the spread. CNKO's gross profit is the difference between a dollar-denominated coal purchase cost and a rupiah selling price that is capped and reset with a lag [S3, S6]. If Newcastle stays at the spot level of US$150.3 rather than falling to our US$118.0 forecast, the FY2027 margin recovery does not happen, and the equity value falls toward the bear case [S0, S6]. The first half of 2026 is the evidence: revenue was broadly flat but gross profit halved [S4]. A prolonged high coal price is the most direct way to lose money in this name.

The second risk is the contract. Two PLN subsidiaries account for essentially all revenue, and the CIF PJBB that runs to 29 October 2029 is the reason the business exists [S2, S4]. A re-tender at a thinner spread, a switch to a different supplier, or a delay in the offtake schedule would hit volumes and margin at the same time. The company's FY2026 delivery target is the contract quantity, below the FY2025 shipment, which tells us the book is being run for spread rather than growth [S2, F3, F4, F73]. We treat contract loss as the central bear case, not a remote tail: the bear scenario assumes no renewal after October 2029 and is valued at nil.

The third risk is the supplier. PT Borneo Indobara supplies more than half of the coal by value, and coal purchases are the largest cost line [S3]. At June 2026 trade payables were IDR956.8bn, of which IDR595.2bn was owed to Borneo Indobara alone, against IDR600.2bn of purchases from it in the first half [S4]. That payable is roughly two hundred days of cost of revenue and about six months of Borneo Indobara purchases, so it is supplier credit, not a permanent float. A reset to thirty-day terms from that supplier alone would call on roughly five-sixths of the payable, close to one and a half times the market capitalisation, and the group has no undrawn facility to fund it [S4]. The concentration is a structural feature of the business, not a temporary condition, and it is the reason the company has little bargaining power.

The fourth risk is the balance sheet. The group has negative equity, a working-capital deficit and a bank loan secured on its receivables [S3, S4]. The June 2026 accounts show the loan being amortised and the factoring line rolling, but the cash is concentrated at the lending bank and IDR379.9bn of deposits received from counterparties are refundable [S4]. If a large supplier demands its deposit back, or the bank refuses to roll the facility, the group would have to fund a repayment from operating cash flow, and the equity could be wiped out before the DCF has time to work. The bear case gives that combined outcome a 30.0% probability; it depends on counterparties we cannot observe, so the probability is a judgement, not a measurement. The offset is genuine: the first half generated IDR102.2bn of operating cash flow and the group met its interest bill, and cash almost covers interest-bearing debt [S4].

The fifth risk is governance. The controlling shareholder arrived in 2024, the group sold one of its two concession-holding subsidiaries to a buyer that was a related party of that subsidiary until the disposal date, the related-party receivable is fully impaired, and the dividend declared for FY2012 is still unpaid [S3, S4]. These are not isolated incidents; they are a pattern that justifies a discount to any valuation. Section six deals with them in detail. A minority holder is relying on the controller's decisions about related-party transactions, capital raising and exit.

The sixth risk is liquidity. The shares trade at a three-month average daily value of IDR0.0bn, the price has ranged from Rp30 to Rp85 over the past year, and the September 2026 release list from the special monitoring board does not include CNKO [S9]. We cannot verify from the public record whether the stock remains on that board; the near-zero traded value means an exit may not be available regardless of the formal status. A holder may not be able to sell at the model value, which is exactly what the 30.0% discount is for. The flip side is that a small buyer can move the price a long way in either direction.

Our base case, with a probability of 50.0%, assumes the deck's coal path, the calibrated pass-through, the current contract book and a renewal of the PJBB beyond October 2029; it produces a twelve-month value of Rp299 before the illiquidity discount [S0, S4]. The bear case, with a probability of 30.0%, assumes no renewal, the H1 spread trough persisting, a failed refinancing and a three-hundred-basis-point higher required return; it produces Rp0, because the equity is worthless once the capital deficiency is closed at a distressed price [S0]. The bull case, with a probability of 20.0%, assumes renewal, a faster normalisation of the coal price and a partial closure of the governance discount; it produces Rp628 [S0]. The asymmetry is deliberate and sourced: the contract caps volume upside within its plus-or-minus band, while the downside includes losing the post-2029 book and a dilutive capital raise.

The signposts that would change our view are concrete. A nine-month result showing gross margin above the second-half level implied by our full-year forecast would support the base case; a margin back above the first-half level would be a large beat. A new PLN contract announcement with a disclosed volume and term would support the bull case. A missed interest payment, a bank demand for accelerated repayment, a qualified going-concern opinion, or a rights issue at a price close to the current one would push us to the bear case or below. A large related-party transaction at a valuation that favours the controller would do the same, regardless of the operating numbers [S3, S4].

Ownership is concentrated and recent. Anderson Bay Pte Ltd held 45.6% at the end of FY2025 and is the controlling shareholder [S2]. The free float is 54.4% and insiders hold 46.1%, leaving a small market for the shares [S0]. The controller's stake was built during the restructuring period, which means the current board and the current strategy are the controller's, not a legacy management team's. That can be positive if the controller injects capital or sells the business; it can be negative if the controller extracts value through related-party transactions.

The audit opinion is unmodified but carries a material-uncertainty paragraph. Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, a member of the BDO network, drew attention to the capital deficiency of IDR1,064.3bn and the excess of current liabilities over current assets of IDR783.1bn at the end of FY2025 [S3]. The opinion is not qualified, which means the auditor believes the accounts give a true and fair view; it does not mean the auditor believes the group will survive without action. The going-concern note sets out management's plan to optimise deliveries under the PLN PJBB that runs to 29 October 2029 [S3, S4]. An investor should read the two statements together: the accounts are reliable as a description of the position, and the position is fragile.

Related-party dealings are material. A receivable of IDR49.4bn from PT Saibatama Internasional Mandiri is fully impaired, and a payable of IDR35.5bn is owed to Mr Andri Cahyadi [S3]. The group also holds security deposits received from counterparties, including IDR324.2bn from PT Sinergi Laksana Bara Mas and IDR93.3bn from PT Berau Coal Energy [S3]. These balances are large relative to the equity and they are not disclosed with the granularity an outside investor would want. The impairment of the receivable is a past loss, but it is also a reminder that related-party credit in this group has not always been recovered.

The disposal of PT Sekti Rahayu Indah deserves scrutiny. The group sold its entire holding to PT Mitra Barito and PT Banua Antang Raya for IDR50.0bn and recognised a gain of IDR62.0bn [S4]. The buyer PT Banua Antang Raya was a shareholder of the subsidiary and was treated as a related party until the disposal date, after which the accounts describe it as a third party [S4]. That is a disclosure fact, not an allegation of wrongdoing, but it means the gain was generated in a transaction with a party that knew the asset. A minority holder should discount the quality of that gain when assessing the FY2026 profit.

Cash and debt sit with the same financial group. Of the IDR338.3bn of cash at June 2026, IDR336.6bn was deposited at PT Bank Sinarmas [S4]. The group's bank loan is from the same bank, and its factoring facility is from PT Sinar Mas Multifinance at a discount rate of 14.0% [S4]. The bank loan is secured by a fiduciary assignment of the PLN receivables [S4]. The practical consequence is that the cash is not a free asset: it is the operating float of a group whose lender can see, and has a claim on, the same cash and receivables. We treat the net debt as small but the liquidity as encumbered.

The dividend record is poor. The company states a 40.0% payout policy, but it paid nothing for FY2025, and the dividend declared for FY2012 of IDR16.3bn is still a liability on the balance sheet [S2, S3]. With negative equity the group has no distributable reserves, so the policy is not a promise an investor should rely on. Our model assumes no dividend through the forecast period [S3].

The exchange status is a live issue. The Indonesia Stock Exchange released a large group of issuers from its special monitoring board in September 2026 after changing the criteria, and CNKO does not appear on that list [S9]. Absence from a release list is not proof of a company's board status, and we cannot verify the status from the public record. What is observable is the near-zero traded value and the thin free float, which mean an exit is effectively unavailable whether or not the formal special-monitoring regime applies [S0, S9]. A release would be a positive catalyst; a suspension would be a negative one.

ESG exposures are dominated by the product and the governance. Coal distribution is a carbon-intensive activity, and the long-run energy transition is a structural headwind for the volume of coal burned in Java [S2]. The company's direct emissions are modest relative to the coal it handles, and its captive plant is small, but the financed and downstream emissions are the relevant measure for a coal distributor. On the social side, the group employs few people and depends on contractors and suppliers, so labour standards are an indirect exposure. Governance is the binding constraint: related-party transactions, a concentrated register, a negative equity position and an unresolved legacy dividend are the issues that matter most to a minority holder.

The annual report gives no capital-raising plan beyond the disposal proceeds, and the investment case rests on the assets and contracts rather than on the quality of the institution [S2, S3]. That is not unusual for an IDX small cap, but it is the reason we value the cash flows rather than impute a strategic premium.

The near catalyst is the nine-month 2026 report, due in the fourth quarter. It will show whether the first-half gross margin was the trough of the coal-price squeeze or the start of a lower-spread regime [S4]. The company's delivery target of 2,000 thousand tonnes for FY2026 gives a volume benchmark [S2], and the house coal deck's FY2026 average of US$137.0 gives a cost benchmark. A gross margin above the second-half level implied by our full-year forecast would support the base case; a margin back above the first-half level would be a large beat; another leg down would push us toward the bear case.

The next catalyst is the FY2026 audited result and the AGM early next year. The audit will show whether the going-concern paragraph is repeated, whether the disposal gain is accepted without adjustment, and whether the group has rebuilt any capital [S3]. The AGM will show whether the board intends to resume dividends or to use the disposal proceeds for debt reduction [S2]. We expect no dividend, but an explicit capital plan would be a positive surprise.

The medium-term catalysts are the debt maturities. The Bank Sinarmas term loan matures in November 2027 and the Sinar Mas Multifinance factoring facility runs to April 2029 [S4]. A clean repayment or refinancing would remove the most visible liquidity risk and would allow the market to value the operating business rather than the balance sheet. A failed refinancing would be the opposite.

We monitor five things between updates. First, tonnes delivered against the FY2026 target and the run-rate in the quarterly accounts [S2]. Second, the gross margin and the spread between the seaborne benchmark and the realised selling price [S3, S6]. Third, trade receivables and the factoring balance, because they determine whether the negative working capital is stable or deteriorating [S4]. Fourth, every related-party disclosure, including new deposits, loans or asset sales [S3]. Fifth, the exchange status and the traded value, because a release from special monitoring or a return of volume would change the discount [S9].

What would make us wrong quickly: the loss of a PLN subsidiary as a customer; a bank demand for accelerated repayment; a qualified audit opinion; a related-party transaction that transfers value away from the listed entity; or a coal price that stays at the spot level long enough to turn the FY2026 margin compression into a permanent condition [S3, S4, S6]. None of those is in the filings today. All of them are plausible enough that the position should be sized for a wide distribution of outcomes, not for the point estimate.
